claims.text: 4.3% of WebText training data contains toxic content from untrustworthy websites.
Certain LLMs exhibit gender biases by associating male names more frequently with career-related words and female names with family-related words.
Prompt injection is designated as the top security threat for LLMs by OWASP.

evidence.description: The authors cite research indicating that 4.3% of WebText data contains toxic content from untrustworthy websites.
Wan, et al. [35] demonstrated that certain LLMs associate male names more frequently with career words and female names with family words in generated reference letters.
The survey notes prompt injection has recently been listed as the top security threat for LLMs by OWASP.

methodologies.name: Literature Survey and Domain Taxonomy
methodologies.description: A comprehensive survey and categorization of existing literature addressing safety concerns in LLMs, specifically targeting ethics, hallucination, prompt injection, data privacy, and societal/legal impacts.

limitations.text: Previous research on recognition and classification of inappropriate content primarily focused on specific forms of malevolence or individual sentences rather than dialogue contexts.
Existing hallucination benchmarks often resort to constrained generation techniques that do not align with unbounded text generation in real-world applications.
LLMs exhibit relatively weak capabilities in distinguishing between system task instructions and user inputs.

future_work.text: Developing stronger privacy-preserving techniques for LLMs.
Investigating the impact of different training data sources on privacy risks.
Exploring mechanisms for user control and consent in LLM deployments to enhance transparency.
Developing legal frameworks that allocate liability and responsibility in LLM deployments.
